item.title: [andros.dev] I built a forum with no interface, no passwords, made for the terminal
item.description:
I like forums. Debates, questions, answers, opinions, etc. That feeling of an asynchronous community, where answers are thought through and content lasts, is what makes the internet an interesting place. That is why I like reading them and taking part in them. But I had never designed or built one. In my spare time I started sketching one, and I ended up building my humble headless, federated forum, with simple, modern technologies and open standards.

And I learned a lot along the way. A forum looks simple, but it hides the classic problems of any server. Who can do what? How do you tell a moderator from a regular user? What happens when you have to ban someone? How do you stop someone from stealing an account? Roles, permissions, bans and security. I had to solve them one by one, and you don't learn that by reading.

Let me tell you how I made Tyrtulia.

A forum with no interface

The server only offers a solid, documented API. It is REST with hypermedia: the client only knows one route, GET /, and discovers everything else by following links. Underneath there are some very boring standards:

  • RFC 9110: HTTP semantics, with ETag and If-Match so edits don't overwrite each other.
  • RFC 9457: errors.
  • RFC 7396: partial updates with PATCH.
  • RFC 6570: URL templates.
  • RFC 4287: Atom feeds.
  • RFC 9562: UUIDv7 identifiers.
  • JSON Schema: validation.
  • Server-Sent Events: real-time events.

There is no web interface, no forms, no advanced authentication systems, no file handling (images, attachments, etc.), and nothing that isn't strictly needed to read and write messages.

That is why it is so light. It uses between 60 and 70 MB of RAM and about 50 MB of disk. It only needs Python and SQLite to run.

An API that discovers itself

How does a client know what it can do? The server tells it with links. Look at the same request, GET /, made by a guest (simplified):

{
    "name": "Forum of example.org",
    "_links": {
        "self": {"href": "/", "method": "GET"},
        "latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},
        "search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},
        "login": {"href": "/sessions", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/session"}
    }
}

And now by alice, logged in:

{
    "name": "Forum of example.org",
    "_links": {
        "self": {"href": "/", "method": "GET"},
        "latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},
        "search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},
        "createThread": {"href": "/threads", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/thread"},
        "notifications": {"href": "/notifications", "method": "GET"},
        "events": {"href": "/events", "method": "GET", "type": "text/event-stream"}
    }
}

If I change a route tomorrow, no client breaks, because none of them knew it in advance. They just follow the links the server gives them.

Why not use one that already exists?

I know there are very complete free software forums:

  • Discourse: the most popular one today.
  • Flarum: PHP with MySQL.
  • NodeBB: Node.js, with MongoDB, Redis or PostgreSQL. It stands out for real time with WebSockets.

Or the good old classic: phpBB.

They are all fantastic, but they are designed to be used from a web browser. They also have an ambitious scope. That is ideal for large communities, but too much for a small, light forum.

That said, Tyrtulia doesn't give up on the browser: it can be indexed by search engines and anyone can read it on the web.

No passwords

No OAuth, no OpenID, no sign-up forms. There are two ways to authenticate:

  • Your Unix user: the client talks to the forum through a Unix socket. The operating system tells the forum which user is on the other side. No sign-up, no login. Your user is your account.
  • SSH key: the client connects over HTTP and the forum sends it a challenge. The client signs it with your private SSH key and the forum verifies it with your public key.

There is no registration over HTTP. If you have a Unix user on the server, you already have an account: it is created the first time you connect through the socket. From there you can add your SSH keys to log in from outside. If you don't have a user on the machine, the administrator creates an account for you with your public key from the command line. On a tilde, having a Unix user is already the invitation.

Easy to use, secure, and no passwords to steal.

What changes compared to BBJ

The idea isn't mine. I was inspired by BBJ, a bulletin board for the terminal built for small communities or clubs (tildes, pubnixes, club servers, etc.). I took its spirit and brought it to my own ground. Still, there are important differences.

First, the foundations.

BBJ Tyrtulia
API style RPC: everything is POST /api/<endpoint> REST with hypermedia (HAL): only GET / is known
Permissions The client asks (is_admin, edit_query) Links that appear or disappear
Authentication Unsalted SHA-256 hash of the password on every request No passwords: Unix socket or SSH-signed challenge
Errors 6 custom numeric codes RFC 9457 with a catalog of types
Pagination Everything at once Cursor based
Concurrency The last edit wins, silently ETag and If-Match
Text format Custom language ([bold: ...], [red: ...]) Standard Markdown
Validation A db_validate endpoint JSON Schema linked from each form
Configuration config.json TOML

Then, the features I missed.

BBJ Tyrtulia
Reply to a specific post >>N quotes in the text Linked replies, with a tree view
Mentions No Yes
Notifications No (pending since 2017) Inbox with replies, mentions and alerts
Real time No, you have to poll Server-Sent Events, with resume
Edit history No, editing overwrites Full, with diffs and revert
Deletion Deletes the row Tombstone: numbering is preserved
Search Each client searches what it has downloaded Server-side full text, accent and case insensitive
Feeds No Atom for the forum and each thread
Moderation Admin or not Roles, hidden posts, reports and a public log
Rate limiting No Per user and per IP

What they share is a small server built on SQLite and several text clients against a documented API.

Clients

A headless forum needs clients, no way around it.

Tyrtulia TUI

Tyrtulia TUI is the terminal client, built with Textual.

tyrtulia.el

If you know me a little, you know this package was a must: tyrtulia.el.

Tyrtulia Web

Tyrtulia Web is more a mirror of the content than a client. Its goal is to let search engines index the forum and let anyone read it from a browser.

It has an unstyled theme and another one that mimics my website.

Federation

You can connect to one forum or set up several. Federation happens in the clients: servers don't talk to each other or copy messages between them. Each forum is independent, with its own users, rules and moderators.

Instead of splitting them into tabs or accounts, the clients mix the threads of all of them into a single list.

Of course, you can only write in the forums where you have an account. In the rest you can only read.

I think it's a pretty cool feature, because it keeps the API code much simpler and lets you explore other forums at zero cost.

Try it

It has been fun to design and build. Of course there are more complete forums, more powerful federation systems, and even decentralized systems that leave Tyrtulia in the dust (Aether, Nostr...). But its niche is very specific: a light, closed-access, federated, indexable, secure forum with text clients. For everything else, there are better things out there.

If you feel like trying it, the installation guide is in the Tyrtulia repository.

I look forward to your feedback.

item.title: [andros.dev] Where do I publish: HTTP, Gopher or Gemini?
item.description:
I agree with McLuhan: the medium, in this case the protocol, is part of the message. Switching protocols is not just a technical decision, it also changes the way people read. The audience is not the same. Neither is the time they spend reading you or exploring your site.

An HTML site carries a mental load: standards, a good DOM design, optimizations (like images), CSS styles, responsive design for different devices, etc. On Gemini or Gopher, on the other hand, you can afford to relax. You follow a syntax that is easy to remember or look up, and you focus on what you want to write. The reader relaxes too, because they know what they will find before they get there.

Answering the question is like choosing between a car and a bike. The bike is worse at almost everything: it is slower, carries less and you get wet. But the experience is personal: you maintain it yourself, you ride along small paths and you notice more of what is around you.

So, to answer the question:

  • HTTP: a large audience. Millions of sites, with very powerful browsers and lots of options.
  • Gemini: an indie audience, with friendly browsers like Lagrange.
  • Gopher: a technical audience, who almost always read from the terminal.

For me, the most amazing thing is the gift we receive from those who write in a Gemini capsule or a Gopher hole (gopherhole). They publish for a few dozen users in a niche. Their texts tend to have a very high quality or a freedom that is hard to find. They are not looking for visits, only to share, selflessly and with deep care for their work. They probably enjoy the journey more than their readers enjoy the result. It is so much like writing free software! You give without knowing who will receive it.

Help me keep writing Every coffee gives me a push toward the next article. Sure, it's on me!

item.title: [adamj.eu] Zsh: uncover hidden files in globs with (D)
item.description:
By default, Zsh globs skip hidden files and directories, meaning those with names starting with a dot. For example, in a project directory, * misses all the configuration files and directories:

$ ls -d *
README.rst  generate_pigeon.py

To include them, add the (D) glob qualifier, which stands for “dot files”:

$ ls …

item.title: [hugovk.dev] Change macOS light and dark mode via command line
item.description:
I normally have my macOS set to dark mode because developer, but sometimes I need to take screenshots for talk slides. For readability and accessibility, it’s important to have enough contrast, and often dark text on a light background is best.

Aliases #

Rather than having to click 🍎 > System Settings… > Appearance > Light, here’s a couple of aliases to do it from the command line:

alias light-mode='osascript -e "tell app \"System Events\" to tell appearance preferences to set dark mode to false"'
alias dark-mode='osascript -e "tell app \"System Events\" to tell appearance preferences to set dark mode to true"'

Then I can type light-mode, take the screenshot, and then go back with dark-mode.

See also #

Some info on accessible presentations:

  • GOV.WALES: How to create accessible PowerPoint presentations

  • W3C Web Accessibility Initiative: Making Events Accessible

item.title: [andros.dev] Tildes: the shared Unix computers
item.description:
Imagine a computer running somewhere. You connect over SSH with your key. A Unix environment appears in front of you, and pwd shows that you are in your own home directory. You type who and see other people logged into the same machine as you. You don't know who they are, but you can finger them and read their .plan. You can even run write to send them a message that will pop up in their terminal. Someone replies that there is an IRC server where everyone hangs out. You run weechat and join the conversation. They say hello. One user tells you there is more documentation on the "forum", a bulletin board, and that you can open it with bbj. You find plenty of information. Reading the threads, you discover that you have a personal website in ~/public_html, published at https://server/~user/. You quickly run nano ~/public_html/index.html and write a few lines of HTML. You check how it looks with lynx. You send an internal email with alpine to the IRC contact who helped you earlier, thanking them and inviting them to visit your new site. While you wait for an answer, you open tin, the news reader (NNTP), to catch up on the news of your small community.

This is not nostalgia for the 90s: it exists today, and it is called a tilde.

What is a tilde

A tilde is a shared, public access Unix computer. Its admin gives you an account, you log in over SSH and you get your own home directory, your shell, your website, your email and your programs. Resources are shared with the rest of the users: the CPU, the disk, the installed programs, and so on.

It is not a platform, a service or a protocol. It is a machine with Unix, an admin and a community.

Paul Ford, the creator of tilde.club, put it like this:

Tilde.club is one cheap, unmodified Unix computer on the Internet.

In practice, almost all of them share these features:

  • A shell account: you log in with ssh user@server and work in the terminal as if it were your own computer.
  • A personal website: whatever you save in ~/public_html is published at https://server/~user/.
  • A local community: IRC chat, internal email, terminal forums and classic commands to see who is online.

They are non-profit: they run on donations and on the time of one or more volunteer admins. And this works because they are small servers, from a dozen to a few thousand users.

Why it is called a tilde

Because of the ~ symbol. On Unix, the tilde stands for your home directory. As Paul Ford said, it is a little like the @ on Twitter, a shortcut that says "here is a person".

Here is an anecdote you can tell your grandchildren. That use of the tilde comes from the Lear-Siegler ADM-3A terminal from the 1970s, where the ~ key and the Home key were the same.

The Tildeverse

The Tildeverse describes itself as "a loose association of like-minded tilde communities". There is no central authority. Each server has its own admins and rules, but they share services and interests. One tilde may only offer Gemini and Gopher, while another has IRC, Mastodon and live radio. The key is that users can move between them and meet: it is a federation of servers, not of applications.

As I write these lines, it has 13 members: aussies.space, cosmic.voyage, ctrl-c.club, envs.net, rw.rs, texto-plano.xyz, tilde.club, tilde.green, tilde.guru, tilde.institute, tilde.pink, tilde.team and tilde.town. If you like to poke around, the full list is available as JSON, with the creation date, operating system and admins of each one. There is a bit of everything: Debian, Fedora, OpenBSD, FreeBSD and even NetBSD.

On top of the servers there is a layer of shared services:

  • tilde.chat: the Tildeverse IRC network (irc.tilde.chat, port 6697 with TLS), with web chat, an XMPP gateway and a Mumble server.
  • tilde.zone: a Mastodon instance for tilde users.
  • tilde.news: a link aggregator in the style of Hacker News.
  • tilderadio.org: a radio station with live DJs. "It's radio minus radio."
  • tildegit.org: a Git forge for community projects.
  • Also: a terminal forum (bbj), a zine, a shared journal, a pastebin and Gopher space.

Nobody forces you to use every service, to socialize or to explore the Tildeverse. But the fun is in bumping into people from your server or from others.

House rules

Each tilde has its own code of conduct, and almost all of them fit in one line. This is tilde.club's:

No drama. Be respectful. Have fun.

tilde.town's is even shorter: "Be kind to each other". But behind the brevity there are clear rules:

  • No cryptocurrency mining: on tilde.town it means an immediate and permanent ban.
  • Nothing commercial: your web space is not for business or advertising.
  • Don't hog resources: the machine belongs to everyone. Don't use it as a backup drive, a proxy or a backend for your IDE.
  • No port scanning and no VPNs: tilde.team bans them, and it has also added a very 2026 rule: no AI agents or services on the server.

My favorite is the motto of texto-plano.xyz, the Spanish-speaking tilde: "let's be few but united". It sums up the philosophy better than any manifesto. A small community is not a limitation, it is the goal. That is why signup forms ask what interests you about the server: they want to make sure there is a curious human being on the other side.

Tildes to explore

Here is my list of active tildes, with their website, approximate number of users and some notes. It may be different tomorrow, but you can keep in mind that the most popular one is tilde.town, with almost 4,000 users.

# Tilde Approx. users Notes
1 tilde.town ~3,900 Very active, its own IRC
2 tilde.club ~3,000 to 4,400 The original, news in 2026
3 tilde.team ~2,400 Wiki, webmail, IRC
4 envs.net ~1,560 Lots of services
5 sdf.org No public list The oldest (1987), has Mastodon
6 tilde.institute ~950 OpenBSD
7 ctrl-c.club ~825 From 2014, latest news in 2023
8 rw.rs ~217 Signups through GitHub
9 tilde.green ~158 Open signups, wiki
10 texto-plano.xyz ~80 In Spanish: radio, podcast and magazine
11 tilde.guru ~67 FreeBSD
12 tilde.fun ~40 Small
13 aussies.space 11 Tiny
14 cosmic.voyage No list Collaborative science fiction
15 republic.circumlunar.space No list Gopher, web and Gemini hosting
16 rawtext.club No list Rebuilding from scratch
17 tilde.pink No list Gopher and Gemini only
18 blinkenshell.org No list Active wiki
19 dimension.sh No list Little visible activity
20 hashbang.sh No list Online

SDF deserves a special mention. It is the grandfather of them all, with almost 40 years behind it, and it works with a different model: the basic account is free, and a one-time fee of $36 (ARPA) gives you lifetime access to more services.

Not everything is pretty

Tildes are machines with people behind them, and that comes with risks.

In May 2026, tilde.town had to close access because of a kernel vulnerability with no patch available. It opened, closed and reopened over two weeks, disabling kernel modules and replacing Nginx with Caddy.

In August it was tilde.team's turn. Someone got root access and ran rm -rf /. Daily backups limited the loss to a few hours, but they had to disable SSH and move the shared Tildeverse services to another machine.

Sharing a computer with thousands of strangers has a price:

  • You depend on the admin. If they get tired, fall ill or lose interest, the server disappears. Grex closed in 2023 after 32 years, and the list of dead tildes is long.
  • Root sees everything. Your files live on someone else's machine. Don't keep secrets there.
  • Security is shared. A kernel bug or a compromised account affects the whole community.
  • Your identity is borrowed. ~user@server is yours as long as the server exists, just like an account on a Mastodon instance.

These are risks you should know and accept before requesting your account.

Final notes

Tildes are a corner that makes the internet a nicer place: you log in, say hello, see who is around, learn new commands, edit your website and read the news. A place shared with people as curious as you.

In 2014, Paul Ford wrote that when people talk about "cloud computing" they are talking about "millions of tiny ghost towns": servers running where nobody lives. A tilde is the exact opposite: a small town that smells of coffee, with neighbors who greet and help each other.

If you end up joining a tilde, I would love to finger you. ;)

Sources

  • Tilde.Club: I had a couple drinks and woke up with 1,000 nerds, Paul Ford's account (October 9, 2014) of how tilde.club was born. His quotes come from here: the cheap Unix computer, the ~ as the @ and the ghost towns of the cloud.
  • tilde.club: its code of conduct, its signup form and its wiki, where the commands in the introduction come from: the command line guide (bbj, lynx, alpine, nano), the IRC page (weechat) and the tin page.
  • Tildeverse, its member list and the JSON version.
  • tilde.chat, tilde.zone, tilde.news, tilderadio.org and tildegit.org, the shared services of the Tildeverse.
  • tilde.town: its code of conduct and its blog, with the May 2026 kernel vulnerability lockdown.
  • tilde.team, with the notice about the August 2026 attack and its terms of service.
  • texto-plano.xyz and its code of conduct.
  • SDF Public Access Unix System on Wikipedia, for its history, and the SDF join page, for current prices.
  • The Grex shutdown notice from 2023 and its history.
  • Tilde on Wikipedia, on the origin of ~ as the home directory and the ADM-3A terminal.
  • I checked the user counts and the status of each tilde by visiting their websites and user lists on October 19, 2026.

item.title: [hugovk.dev] Releasing Python 3.15.0
item.description:
Prologue #

Like last year, I livetooted the release of Python 3.15.0. Here it is in blogpost form!

Two weeks #

Two weeks until Python 3.15.0 final!

#Python #Python315
Fri, Sep 18, 2026, 00:30 EEST

One week #

One week until Python 3.15.0 final!!

What are you most looking forward to?

#Python #Python315
Tue, Sep 22, 2026, 21:17 EEST

Python 3.15.0 release day! #

First blocker, we’re getting 503s on docs.python.org and buildbot.python.org, the latter of which is needed to check the tier 1 and 2 buildbots are passing, needed for a release.

It’s a certificate issue from an incompatible pyOpenSSL upgrade. We’re waiting for the US to wake up and poke it with a stick.

#Python #Python315
Thu, Oct 1, 2026, 14:19 EEST

Red #

The US woke up and they’re both back up!

Now, there’s one tier 1 failure to check.

#Python #Python315 #release
Thu, Oct 1, 2026, 14:22 EEST

Flaky #

RuntimeError: join took too long: <Process name='Process-2107' pid=2290504 parent=2276730 started daemon>

Looks like a flaky test, and python/cpython#157184 has a fix to increase a timeout. Will try restarting for now.

#Python #Python315 #release
Thu, Oct 1, 2026, 14:25 EEST

Green #

That passed, the buildbots are back to green ✅️

Next, issues/PRs with release-blocker label.

One is a straightforward docs update, I marked as blocker so I don’t forget, to change future tense to present.

Then three last-minute lazy import blockers that need a closer look.

#Python #Python315 #release
Thu, Oct 1, 2026, 15:11 EEST

Traditional surprise rc3 #

Following recent tradition, I’m going to add a surprise third release candidate!

It makes sense to include the last-minute lazy-import fixes in 3.15.0 final.

It also makes sense to give time to test them properly, so today’s planned 3.15.0 final is postponed, and I’m going to release a 3.15.0rc3 tomorrow, assuming everything is in place.

And then 3.15.0 final will follow about week later. Exact date to be announced.

We’re nearly there! 🤞

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 00:49 EEST

Missing backport #

The three lazy blockers are finally merged into main, two have been backported to 3.15, but wait, the third failed, because it depends on some tests not yet backported.

Okay, backport created, merge conflict fixed, CI is now spinning, and automerge enabled. That’ll merge in about 15 mins, then we can update it into the last blocker PR, that should merge about 30 mins later, and rc3 can begin!

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 20:58 EEST

rc3 #

Get yer rc3 here!

You know the drill: please test and report bugs!

Library maintainers, join the Cool Testers’ Club 😎 and add 3.15 to your test matrix.

Python 3.15.0 final planned for 2026-10-09.

#Python #Python315 #release
Sat, Oct 3, 2026, 00:14 EEST

Python 3.15.0 release day (second attempt)! #

✅️ Release date updated in What’s New in Python 3.15

✅️ No release blockers

✅️ No deferred blockers

✅️ Buildbots all green

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 13:03 EEST

Cooldowns #

Pydantic finally added support for Python 3.15 yesterday, and aiohttp on Monday, so I could use Python 3.15 rc3 to run the release scripts and release Python 3.15.0 final!

But… I’m going to respect our seven-day cooldown, and stick with 3.14.

You also use cooldowns for your dependencies, right?

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 13:12 EEST

blurb bug #

Pushing the big launch button:

.venv/bin/python run_release.py --repository ../cpython --ssh-user hugovk --release 3.15.0

… and immediately ran into a bug with our changelog tool blurb, because we’ve had no new NEWS fragments since rc3 :)

This needs a fix in blurb, a new PyPI release, and then the docs lockfile regenerated and backported to 3.15.

Fix PR: python/blurb#92

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 13:43 EEST

blurb fix #

OK, merged and released (really easy using Trusted Publishing), lockfile updated and backported.

Restarted the release and that’s better now.

A temporary branch and tag has been pushed to my fork, and I need to verify the release commit does not contain any unexpected changes.

All looks good. Next to start the installer and artifact builds.

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 14:21 EEST

Installers #

The release artifact build failed, need to bump blurb in that lockfile too.

Like this: python/release-tools#451

Now restarted that workflow with the existing CPython tag, no need for retag.

This builds source+docs tarballs and Android+iOS artifacts. Takes ~30 mins.

Ned Deily has started the macOS installer builds. And I’ve started the Windows installer builds, takes ~2 hours.

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 14:56 EEST

SBOM #

In the meantime, the GitHub Actions build has finished, SBOMs created and some things uploaded.

The Windows process has paused a couple of times, awaiting button clicks to approve signing of binaries. The whole release team gets emails about this, so no sneaking out signed releases. 🥷

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 16:04 EEST

Nearly there #

Windows complete, tags pushed upstream, Sigstore signing done, adding files to python.org… nearly there…

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 17:11 EEST

Out now #

🐍🚀 Out now: Python 3.15.0 final!

💤 Lazy imports!
🧊 frozendict builtin!
💂 sentinel builtin!
📉 Tachyon profiler!
🖼️ Frame pointers everywhere!
🛅 Unpacking in comprehensions!
🗣️ UTF-8 as the default encoding!
🛞 Stable ABI for free-threading!
🆕 Package startup config files!
⌨️ TypedDict & TypeForm!
🐎 Faster JIT!
🎨 More colour!
🚌 & more!

Huge thanks to the Sovereign Tech Agency supporting my work as release manager and enabling another smooth release!

#Python #Python315 #CPython #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 17:23 EEST

It’s not over yet! #

I updated PEP 790, which also updates the PEPs API, which is used to point the docs at /3/ to 3.15, kicked off a docs build: docs.python.org/3/

Unpin one toot and pin another to my profile.

(3.14 might not be the newest, but we can still celebrate with pie!)

And then unlock the 3.15 branch so the core team can start merging 185 PRs that didn’t get in during RC.

#Python #Python315 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 18:27 EEST

Also #

✅️ update 3.15 label
✅️ rebuild devguide to update: devguide.python.org/versions/
✅️ unlock 3.15 branch

And I think that’s it!

Hey, @savannah, you’re up next with the first 3.16 alpha on Tuesday! 🚀

#Python #Python315 #Python316 #release
Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 18:58 EEST

item.title: [andros.dev] The Photoshop clone that hurts GIMP
item.description:
We are seeing a wave of "X rebuilt in pure Y" projects: clones of the most expensive proprietary software. In just a few weeks, someone has published a replica of almost the entire Adobe and Microsoft Office catalog, written in Rust by Claude. PhotoCraft, a Photoshop clone. WordCraft, a Word clone. FigCraft, a Figma clone. And more projects are on the way.

From a distance, it may look like a checkmate against companies like Adobe or Microsoft. In reality, it is a move against open source. We are building free alternatives to free software, not to proprietary software. Professionals pay for the license because they want things to work and be compatible; they don't care about alternatives. Whoever installs a clone is someone who never wanted to pay Adobe in the first place. The same person who would have downloaded GIMP or Krita. A user who could have discovered a free project, and maybe even contributed to it one day, ends up with a broken version and no support.

Behind every open source project there are years or decades of accumulated knowledge, of very specific and very specialized contributions. GIMP was born in 1995 as a class project by two Berkeley students, and LibreOffice descends from StarWriter, a word processor from 1985. Every fixed line has a story behind it: a document that broke its layout, a printer that didn't work properly, a .docx with twenty years of inherited styles. A clone can imitate the behavior it observes, but not the accumulated wisdom.

Then there is the lack of friction. Without the effort of learning or contributing, there is no long-term bond, let alone a community. I wrote about this in I closed pull requests and issues on my projects, and I'm happier, in case you want to dig deeper. A project needs frustration, reward and communication to be sustainable. Whoever drops a prompt into your project today will drop it into a more fun one tomorrow.

I'm not against using AI to code: I use it every day. I'm against where the effort is going. All that energy, all that money spent on tokens, could be fixing the interface or the documentation of an existing project, or improving its compatibility. But contributing to something old is boring, and cloning popular software is fun: it gives you the feeling of having beaten Adobe over a weekend. Meanwhile, the one really getting weaker is the free software ecosystem.

Free software isn't defended by cloning it. It's defended by using it and contributing to it. Instead of inviting people to use a clone, buy a virtual coffee for the developer behind your favorite free alternative.

Help me keep writing Every coffee gives me a push toward the next article. Sure, it's on me!

item.title: [andros.dev] We don't want decentralized systems, we want small ones
item.description:
We don't want distributed systems, we want small systems. It doesn't matter if they are centralized inside: what matters is that they stay at a manageable size. That makes them cheap, easy to maintain and almost free of moderation. One example is tildes, shared Unix servers where every user has their own account. They run on a trusted admin and donations. When they grow too big, more tildes appear. Another example is Friend Camp, a community of friends. It costs about $30 a month, around $1 per person.

Despite being centralized, they feel like the opposite of big platforms. There are no commercial interests and people know each other. It's like a shoe shop in a small town. The shop can only serve a few customers because there is little space, you know the owner's name (maybe even his wife's) and the shelves don't offer much variety; and yet you know you will be well served and the owner wants you to leave with what is best for you. In a big department store, on the other hand, the staff don't care whether you come back or not. The owner might be a board of shareholders who only want to maximize profit. Space is unlimited, but there are queues and it's hard to get help. You don't even know if the product is what you are looking for, even if it is cheaper. Welcome to economies of scale. Now apply that to centralized systems.

Distributed systems make us feel in control, because resources are shared among all participants. In return, they only ask us to provide the hardware and the time to maintain it. And that is where they clash with what Moxie Marlinspike said: "People do not want to run their own servers" (2022). Maybe we don't have the time, the money or the knowledge to be a node in a distributed network. Maybe we already have enough with our lives without also having to keep an eye on our mail server. So we end up using a centralized provider inside a distributed system: GitHub or GitLab when we want to use Git, Gmail or Outlook when we want to use email, or WordPress.com or Medium when we want to publish a blog. The small system solves the dilemma without giving up what matters: one person provides the server and the time for everyone else, and the rest only need to trust someone they know. Isn't that too much load for one person? Not if the community is small. Darius Kazemi, with about 50 active users on Friend Camp, gets on average one moderation request a month.

Take three Mastodon instances as an example: icosahedron.website (about 133 monthly active users), mastodon.technology (about 23,600 accounts) and mastodon.social (about 3.4 million accounts). All three run the same software and the same protocol; the only thing that changes is size. The second one shut down in 2022 because its only admin burned out. The other two are still alive, but for different reasons: the first because it is small, and the third because it has plenty of resources (in 2024, the organization that runs it brought in about 2.19 million euros, almost all of it from donations).

The biggest risk for a volunteer-run community is almost always the same: that whoever maintains it burns out. That is why size is not a detail: it is what keeps the work within what one person can handle. Limiting size with waiting lists, closed registrations or a cap on active users seems counterintuitive, but it works. To grow without burning out, there are only two paths left: raise a lot of money, like mastodon.social, or become a business, like Reddit, X or YouTube. But profit guarantees neither better quality nor better service. My small Forgejo instance is as centralized as GitHub, but it has 10 active users: it has gone down fewer times, it is faster and it costs me pennies a month to run.

Leopold Kohr wrote it in 1957, long before the internet existed: "Wherever something is wrong, something is too big". Maybe we have spent years asking the wrong question. It doesn't matter so much whether a system is centralized, federated or distributed. What matters is whether it fits in the hands of someone you can write to when something breaks. Paul Ford, when he said goodbye to tilde.club, put it in writing: "you can, at any time, for very little money and relatively little effort, stand up a tiny digital community that basically belongs to itself".

So next time you are looking for a place to publish, to host your code or to talk with your friends, don't ask whether it is decentralized. Ask how many people are inside and whether you know the name of the person who runs it.

Sources

  • Paul Ford on tilde.club, the creator of the first tilde (2014). In his 2019 note he hands the server over to new admins, along with a waiting list of 10,000 people.
  • I had a couple drinks and woke up with 1,000 nerds, Paul Ford's account (2014) of how tilde.club was born and the flood of accounts in its first days.
  • Tildeverse, the association of tildes that followed the tilde.club model.
  • tilde.club, a shared Unix computer funded by its users' donations.
  • texto-plano.xyz, a Spanish-speaking tilde: "seamos pocos pero unidos" (let us be few but united).
  • Run your own social, Darius Kazemi's guide based on Friend Camp: 50 to 100 active users, one moderation request a month and about $30 a month in costs.
  • My first impressions of web3, Moxie Marlinspike's article, the source of the quote "People do not want to run their own servers".
  • Icosahedron, a Mastodon instance running since February 2017 with closed registrations.
  • Dear mastodon.technology community, the shutdown announcement by Ash Furrow, who ran it alone.
  • Archive Team: Mastodon, a record of closed instances, including mastodon.technology and its 23,600 accounts.
  • mastodon.social, the largest Mastodon instance, run by the developers of the software themselves.
  • Mastodon Annual Report 2024, the accounts of Mastodon gGmbH: revenue, costs and moderation of mastodon.social.
  • The Breakdown of Nations, Leopold Kohr's book (1957), the source of the quote "Wherever something is wrong, something is too big".

It can be hard for us developers to keep track of all of them, with their different support policies and end-of-life dates, and running an unsupported version means missing …
